question: Can score-based diffusion models be defined and trained directly on inequality-constrained domains so that both noising and denoising remain feasible, using either an interior log-barrier geometry or boundary reflection, and do those constructions work on polytopes, trace-constrained positive-definite matrices, robotics, and cyclic-peptide conformations?

key_findings.claim: The paper's substantive contribution is a two-route constrained-diffusion framework: an interior log-barrier Langevin process and a reflected Brownian process, coupled to reverse-time score dynamics, implicit score matching, and constraint-aware random walks.
key_findings.evidence: For an inequality domain M={x:f_i(x)<0}, the barrier route sets g=nabla^2 phi and evolves dX=(1/2)div(g^{-1})dt+g^{-1/2}dB; its reverse adds g^{-1} times the score. The reflection route solves a Skorokhod problem with an outward-normal bounded-variation term, reverses it with the score drift, and discretizes geodesic steps by repeated reflection. Both use an implicit score-matching objective because their transition scores are unavailable in closed form. This is a useful constructional package, although later findings below qualify several formal statements.

anchors.section: Barrier forward/reverse processes, Equations 9-11 and Algorithm 1

key_findings.claim: The printed log-barrier definition has a sign error, while the appendix assumptions used to justify its existence, ergodicity, and density are literally incompatible with the paper's canonical open domains.
key_findings.evidence: For Ax<b, Equation 6 prints -sum_i log(<A_i,x>-b_i), whose logarithm receives a negative slack; it should use b_i-<A_i,x>. Equation 8 does use the correct slack S=diag(b_i-<A_i,x>), confirming the inconsistency. More seriously, Assumption A1 declares M a compact subset of R^d, whereas Section 2 defines nonempty M by strict inequalities and hence open. If M instead means its compact closure, a log-barrier inverse metric degenerates at the boundary and cannot remain positive definite there as A1 requires. Proposition C.3 also claims a smooth density for t>=0 despite C.1 starting at a fixed x0, so t=0 is a Dirac mass. The cited propositions therefore do not establish the advertised canonical barrier setting as written.

anchors.section: Appendix C, Assumption A1 and Propositions C.1-C.3

key_findings.claim: The reflected implicit-score argument needs only zero normal flux, but the paper imposes and implements the much stronger condition that the entire score vector vanish throughout a boundary strip.
key_findings.evidence: A reflected heat density satisfies a Neumann condition, so <nabla log p,n>=0 on the boundary; tangential score components need not vanish. Proposition 3.3 instead assumes s(t,x)=0 as a vector for every boundary point, while its integration-by-parts proof exposes the actual boundary term as <s,n>p. The implemented parameterization multiplies every score component by min(1,ReLU(d(x,boundary)-delta)), plus a tiny code epsilon, making the whole vector approximately zero for d<=delta. Thus the practical class generally cannot represent the true tangential score near the boundary, and global recovery of the correct score under that class is too strong.

anchors.section: 3.2, reflected heat equation and Neumann condition

key_findings.claim: The appendix's reflected probability-flow proposition has the wrong score sign and an internally inconsistent proof, even though the preceding main formula has the correct negative sign.
key_findings.evidence: Main Equation 43 uses drift (1/2)div(g^{-1})-(1/2)g^{-1}nabla log p, which has the expected sign. Proposition F.1 then defines dX=+(1/2)nabla log p_t(X)dt and claims the same marginals as reflected Brownian motion. Its continuity equation is partial_t q=-(1/2)div(q nabla log p), the negative of the forward heat equation when q=p. It also states equality for B and an undefined Y although it defines X, and its boundary non-hitting argument asserts Y_t lies on the boundary from smoothness. Consequently the likelihood/ODE derivation is not proved by Proposition F.1 as printed.

anchors.section: Appendix F, Equations 42-43 and Proposition F.1

key_findings.claim: The printed proof of reflected time reversal contains vector-scalar mismatches and does not establish that its constructed martingale is Brownian.
key_findings.evidence: Lemma G.2 Equation 44 integrates a scalar u against vector dk but equates it to a scalar surface integral; a vector identity would require the normal n, or the left side should use d|k|. Equation 57 similarly lacks a normal in a vector boundary term, Equation 58 cites Theorem C.2 where the required boundary identity is Lemma G.2, and Equation 45 attaches membership in M to the unconstrained B. The final step invokes Levy's characterization from E[B_t B_t^T]=tI, but Levy requires quadratic covariation [B^i,B^j]_t=delta_ij t, not merely covariance. It also assumes a reversed/transformed process is strong Markov because the forward process is, which is not automatic. The time-reversal formula may be available from prior probability theory, but this proof is not valid as written.

anchors.section: Appendix G, Definition G.1, Lemma G.2, Equations 44-45
Appendix G, Equations 56-62 and Brownian characterization

key_findings.claim: The Skorokhod appendix reverses its own reflection sign and contains consequential cross-reference errors.
key_findings.evidence: Main Equation 12 and stochastic Theorem D.3 use constrained path = driving path - outward-normal regulator. Deterministic Theorem D.2(c), under the same outward-normal convention, instead prints x+k=bar x. The discussion then says the difference between D.2 and D.3 is in D.3(c), which differs from D.3(c), and says the Brownian case recovers D.3(c) from itself. These are exact source errors, not extraction artifacts, and make the appendix unreliable as a self-contained statement of the sign convention.

anchors.section: Appendix D, Theorem D.3 and discussion

key_findings.claim: The constrained methods guarantee feasibility by construction, but the main controlled benchmark is a negative high-dimensional result: ordinary Euclidean diffusion has much lower MMD at dimension ten.
key_findings.evidence: Table 1 reports 100% in-domain samples for both constrained routes in every hypercube/simplex setting, while Euclidean feasibility falls only from 98.8% to 96.4% on hypercubes and from 96.4% to 92.6% on simplices. At d=10, Euclidean MMD is 0.081+/-0.005 on the hypercube versus 0.330+/-0.004 barrier and 0.313+/-0.048 reflected; on the simplex it is 0.060+/-0.003 versus 0.275+/-0.015 and 0.290+/-0.009. The authors acknowledge that their synthetic target puts less mass near boundaries as dimension grows and that constrained hyperparameters were borrowed from Euclidean experience. Thus the experiment establishes exact feasibility, not competitive high-dimensional density modeling.

key_findings.claim: The SPD application contains two definition/scale errors and supplies only a small qualitative robotics comparison without an unconstrained baseline.
key_findings.evidence: The manuscript defines positive definite matrices with x^T M x>=0, which is the positive-semidefinite condition; strict positivity for nonzero x is required. Under M=LL^T, Tr(M)=sum_ij L_ij^2<C places L in a ball of radius sqrt(C), not radius C as stated. On a 2x2 SPD manipulability matrix plus R^2 position, the reflected model reports MMD 0.161 versus barrier 0.247 and the figures qualitatively trace a letter L; no Euclidean comparator, uncertainty, held-out downstream control test, or physical robot validation is reported.

anchors.section: Appendix H, SPD motivation and parameterization

key_findings.claim: The cyclic-peptide demonstration learns a smoothed force-field-derived surrogate, not empirical protein conformations or a protein-design objective, and its domain dimension is contradictory across the main text and appendix.
key_findings.evidence: The target is constructed by drawing 10^7 uniform C-alpha chains, rebuilding full atoms with PULCHRA, relaxing non-C-alpha atoms, evaluating OpenMM/AMBER potential energy, importance-weighting at 273.15 K, adding Brownian smoothing, and subsampling 10^6 examples. Both constrained models report MMD 0.032 against this computational surrogate, versus 0.112 for uniform. Main Section 5.3, Figures 10 and 25, and the code's n_torus=4 use P^3 x T^4 for a six-link chain; Appendix I.1 derives P x T^(N-3), I.2 explicitly uses P x T^3 for N=6, while Figure 19's caption again says a four-dimensional torus. The exact active TeX contains both variants and does not resolve which mathematical parameterization underlies the result.

key_findings.claim: The formal scope is much narrower than the paper's practical and discussion-level generality claims.
key_findings.evidence: The reflected theory is presented for bounded convex Euclidean domains with smooth boundary, but the core experiments use hypercubes, simplices, and Birkhoff polytopes with corners, as well as product spaces with a torus. Algorithm 2 is stated for generic constrained Riemannian manifolds although no convergence theorem covers its general geodesic-reflection construction. The paper discusses non-convex and non-Euclidean applicability, while its later same-author Metropolis paper explicitly characterizes these original samplers as computationally burdensome or restricted to convex Euclidean sets. Exact feasibility in experiments does not bridge those theorem assumptions.

key_findings.claim: The reflected-step pseudocode and the released implementation expose edge cases that weaken the claimed general discretization.
key_findings.evidence: Algorithm 2 loops while remaining length ell>=0 rather than ell>0, so exact exhaustion can trigger another normalization/reflection step. Algorithm 3 is captioned as discretizing dX=b dt+dB-dk but its displayed step uses only sqrt(gamma)Z, omitting b; the public code does include reverse score drift before passing a combined tangent step to manifold.exp, so the paper's pseudocode rather than the actual reverse path is incomplete. The companion polytope reflection code divides by the step norm without a zero-step guard and caps a bounded while-loop at 100,000 reflections. Barrier sampling replaces the true exponential map by clipping/projection without an approximation bound, which the authors themselves identify as requiring many steps.

anchors.section: Algorithms 2-3 reflected step and random walk

key_findings.claim: The appendix's universal experimental recipe is contradicted by the released experiment configurations, preventing an exact identification of the settings behind reported numbers.
key_findings.evidence: Appendix J states that all models use batch size 256, 100,000 iterations, and beta_max=6. The linked repository instead sets batch_size=1024 for several hypercube/simplex configurations, beta_f values including 7, 15, 35, and 55, 50,001 steps for SPD, and 150,001 steps plus 2,000 diffusion steps for the peptide configuration. Those may be the real per-task settings, but the paper labels its recipe universal and does not map configurations or seeds to Table 1 and the application results. This is a source-to-artifact contradiction rather than a mere missing convenience script.

anchors.section: Appendix J, Architecture, Training, Diffusion, and Metrics

key_findings.claim: The official code release is an archival snapshot, not a self-contained reproducibility artifact.
key_findings.evidence: At public HEAD fbeee12df178ed2e08dd0596e791f0d32a3a8c6a (one commit, dated 2023-08-15), the README requires a modified Geomstats branch but its commands clone the default branch and another score-sde repository; no commit is pinned. Requirements have no versions and include the misspelled hydra-joblib-launche, setup.py comments out install_requires and uses an invalid hyphenated package include, configs contain private /data/ziz paths and a plaintext W&B API credential, and no release, license, lockfile, CI, checkpoints, raw result tables, or result-to-command manifest exists. Static compilation finds a real syntax error in run_product.py and notebook magics in numerous .py files, including a test. The companion Geomstats tmlr branch at b1b23a3be8c7209fa69376fa02779b306dc66b8c is likewise branch-referenced rather than pinned by the artifact. Included data help inspect some tasks, and relevant core modules are readable, but a clean reproduction cannot follow the documented path.

key_findings.claim: The current competitive record narrows the durable novelty to the log-barrier-plus-reflection scientific-domain package rather than reflected diffusion itself or a scalable constrained sampler.
key_findings.evidence: Lou and Ermon's Reflected Diffusion Models was submitted one day earlier, independently derives reverse reflected SDEs, constrained score losses, likelihood and ODE sampling, and scales to images and high-dimensional simplices; the target's v2 acknowledges their ODE priority. Subsequent same-author Metropolis sampling reports substantial efficiency and performance gains over these original samplers; mirror diffusion retains analytic transition tractability on convex sets; reflected Schrodinger bridges add transport structure; projected methods cover nonconvex and physical constraints; and 2025-2026 boundary-conditioned Langevin and reflected bridge-matching work adds convergence-rate or partially simulation-free machinery. The target remains distinctive for presenting both a log-barrier metric route and a reflection route with early robotics/peptide demonstrations.

anchors.section: Appendix F acknowledgment of reflected ODE priority

method.core_idea: Turn inequality constraints into either geometry or boundary dynamics: use the Hessian of a diverging log barrier so an interior diffusion cannot reach the boundary, or use a reflected Brownian motion whose local-time regulator keeps trajectories inside, then learn the corresponding time-dependent score and reverse the process.
method.mechanism: For the barrier model, a strictly convex smooth phi supplies metric g=nabla^2 phi, forward drift (1/2)div(g^{-1}), diffusion g^{-1/2}, and a reverse score term g^{-1}nabla log p; a geodesic random walk with an approximate retraction simulates it. For the reflected model, a Skorokhod regulator subtracts the outward normal whenever a step meets the boundary; time reversal adds a score drift and another regulator. Both models train a sinusoidal MLP with implicit score matching and multiply its output by a distance-to-boundary gate. Product constructions combine a constrained component with ordinary Riemannian diffusion on a torus.
assumptions: The inequality domain and its boundary admit the smoothness, compactness, and nonexplosion properties needed by the cited stochastic-process results.
The barrier is smooth and strictly convex and its Hessian defines a valid complete-enough metric whose inverse and divergence are regular along trajectories.
The reflected-domain time-reversal theorem applies, primarily for bounded convex Euclidean domains with smooth boundary and smooth positive densities.
A distance-to-boundary gate that suppresses the complete learned vector field near the boundary is an acceptable approximation to the true Neumann score condition.
Approximate exponential maps, Euclidean projection/retraction, and repeated specular reflection are accurate at the chosen discretization schedules.
The terminal forward distribution is sufficiently close to uniform that reverse generation can initialize from a tractable uniform law.
MMD on 100,000 samples and qualitative pair/trajectory plots adequately measure distribution recovery in the reported low-dimensional tasks.
Force-field-weighted and smoothed C-alpha conformations constitute a meaningful proof-of-concept target for cyclic-peptide conformational generation.

techniques.role: Uses a log-barrier Hessian metric to define an interior forward diffusion and metric-preconditioned reverse score dynamics.
Keeps the forward and reverse paths feasible with an outward-normal bounded-variation regulator.
Approximates continuous manifold SDEs with tangent Gaussian steps, drift, and a metric exponential or retraction.
Consumes each proposed geodesic step in segments and specularly reflects the remaining direction at intersected constraints.
Trains scores without closed-form transition kernels through norm-plus-divergence score matching and integration by parts.
Multiplies the complete network output by a clipped distance-to-boundary function intended to enforce a zero boundary score.
Combines constrained polytope dynamics with ordinary Riemannian diffusion on a torus for cyclic chains.
Maps trace-constrained SPD matrices to positive-diagonal lower-triangular factors under orthant and norm constraints.
Compares generated and target distributions with RBF-kernel maximum mean discrepancy over 100,000 samples.

limitations: The barrier propositions use a compact-open assumption mismatch and do not prove the canonical log-barrier process as stated.
The reflected time-reversal proof has dimensional and martingale-characterization gaps; its truth must be supplied by stronger external results, not this appendix.
The probability-flow proposition has the wrong sign and inconsistent variables, so reflected likelihood evaluation is not justified by the printed proof.
Full-vector boundary suppression is stronger than Neumann normal-flux enforcement and introduces an unquantified approximation bias in a strip of width delta.
Reflected theory assumes smooth boundaries, while hypercubes, simplices, Birkhoff polytopes, and general inequality intersections have corners or lower-dimensional affine structure.
The main synthetic target becomes effectively more interior as dimension grows; it does not stress high-dimensional boundary mass while constrained MMD degrades sharply.
All principal experiments are low-dimensional; no image-scale, long-chain, high-rank SPD, or otherwise high-dimensional constrained task is demonstrated.
MMD kernel choices are only broadly described, raw run values are absent, and applications lack strong task-specific baselines and downstream utility metrics.
The robotics experiment has no unconstrained comparator, uncertainty, control success, or hardware validation.
The peptide target is generated from one modeling pipeline and smoothed before learning; it is neither an empirical conformational ensemble nor a protein-design benchmark.
The paper contradicts itself on whether the peptide torus has three or four dimensions for N=6.
The trace-constrained SPD text confuses positive definite with semidefinite and ball radius C with sqrt(C).
Repeated reflection and barrier retraction are computationally expensive, and neither practical discretization receives a task-level bias or convergence analysis.
The appendix's one-size-fits-all experimental hyperparameters conflict with the public per-task configurations.
The artifact lacks a portable, pinned, licensed, command-to-result reproduction path and contains syntax, packaging, credential, and dependency defects.
failure_modes: A score field with valid zero normal component but nonzero tangential component is systematically attenuated near the boundary, biasing modes that run along a face.
At polytope corners, simultaneous or nearly simultaneous face hits can make the choice and ordering of specular reflections numerically unstable and nonunique.
A zero tangent proposal causes the released reflection routine to divide by its norm, while exact exhaustion can trigger an extra pseudocode loop.
Capping the number of reflections can return an incompletely consumed proposal for large steps or narrow domains.
Euclidean clipping used as a barrier retraction can place states on the boundary where the intended log-barrier metric is singular.
A terminal distribution insufficiently mixed to uniform creates initialization mismatch in reverse sampling; no terminal-distance diagnostic is reported.
High-dimensional targets concentrated away from the boundary can make an unconstrained model far easier to fit while the constrained geometry adds variance and stiffness.
Trace-factor coordinates can distort distances and density comparisons over SPD matrices, especially near zero diagonals or the norm boundary.
An ambiguous peptide coordinate definition can silently train and evaluate different-dimensional products or mislabel figures while still yielding plausible MMD numbers.
Following the README can install the wrong Geomstats branch; following setup.py can omit the Riemannian package and dependencies; running the product entry point hits a syntax error.
Private absolute data paths and absent result manifests can lead users to run a nearby configuration that is not the one underlying a reported table.
reusable_insights: For constrained generative models, separate three questions: mathematical path feasibility, discretized-sampler feasibility, and density fidelity; 100% valid samples answer only the first two.
A vector-valued Neumann condition constrains only the normal component; imposing a zero vector is a materially different model class and should be ablated against normal projection.
Barrier formulas should be checked against slack signs and the metric matrix; a single unit-interval example exposes impossible logarithms and boundary degeneracy immediately.
Time-reversal proofs should verify quadratic variation, filtration adaptation, and Markov claims explicitly rather than substitute covariance identities.
Probability-flow signs can be audited by inserting q=p into the continuity equation and checking whether it reproduces the forward Fokker-Planck equation.
Experiments on constrained spaces should vary boundary mass independently of ambient dimension, since an interior-concentrated target can favor an unconstrained baseline for the wrong reason.
Product-manifold dimension counts should be traced from parameter indices to config shapes to pair-plot axes; this triangulation exposed the peptide T^3/T^4 contradiction.
A paper-wide hyperparameter paragraph should be mechanically compared with every released task config before being treated as a reproducibility specification.
Artifact review should include companion forks and exact branch commits when core geometry is delegated outside the main repository.
open_questions: Can the barrier existence, ergodicity, and smooth-density results be restated for an open bounded domain with a degenerate inverse metric and proved under assumptions actually satisfied by log barriers?
Can the authors replace the Appendix G proof with a correct reflected time-reversal theorem that covers nonsmooth convex polytopes or state the exact external theorem used?
What is the correct reflected probability-flow ODE and boundary condition, and do likelihood estimates agree with numerical density benchmarks after fixing Proposition F.1?
How much fidelity is lost by zeroing all score components in a boundary strip compared with enforcing only s dot n=0 exactly?
What weak limit does the repeated geodesic-reflection scheme approach at corners, and how does reflection order affect bias?
How do barrier, reflected, Metropolis, and mirror samplers compare at matched compute on targets with controlled high boundary mass and increasing dimension?
Which exact configs, seeds, checkpoints, and raw sample sets produced every Table 1 row and the robotics and peptide MMD values?
Is the cyclic-peptide model P^3 times T^3 or P^3 times T^4, and what is the correct derivation from the number of joints, links, and dihedral indices?
Do peptide samples remain competitive under empirical structural data, stronger molecular simulation, energy/diversity metrics, and experimental or docking validation?
Can a clean, credential-free release pin the constrained-diffusion and Geomstats commits, repair packaging and syntax, and reproduce all reported results end to end?

competitive_landscape.title: Riemannian Score-Based Generative Modelling
competitive_landscape.difference: De Bortoli et al. extend score-based diffusion, time reversal, and score matching to smooth Riemannian manifolds without boundary. The reviewed paper reuses that framework and several authors but targets inequality boundaries through barrier or reflection; its formal and numerical difficulties arise precisely where the predecessor's complete-boundaryless assumptions stop applying.

competitive_landscape.title: Riemannian Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Huang et al. derive continuous-time diffusion, variational likelihood, divergence computation, and Riemannian score matching on smooth manifolds such as spheres, tori, hyperboloids, and orthogonal groups. It does not solve inequality-boundary feasibility; the target adds two boundary mechanisms but does not match that paper's likelihood benchmark coverage.

competitive_landscape.title: Reflected Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Lou and Ermon were submitted one day earlier and independently develop reverse reflected SDEs, constrained denoising/score matching, likelihood training, diffusion guidance, and ODE sampling, scaling to high-dimensional simplices and image benchmarks. The target adds the distinct log-barrier route and scientific product/SPD examples, but reflected diffusion and its probability-flow extension are not unique to it.

competitive_landscape.title: Metropolis Sampling for Constrained Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Fishman et al. explicitly identify the reviewed barrier/reflection samplers as computationally burdensome or convex-Euclidean-only, then introduce a Metropolis discretization of reflected Brownian motion with substantial reported efficiency/performance gains and convex, nonconvex, geospatial, robotics, and protein tasks. It supersedes much of the original practical sampler claim while retaining the target's basic constrained-score motivation.

competitive_landscape.title: Mirror Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Tae proposes mapping constrained continuous and categorical domains through mirror geometry, demonstrating simplex diffusion and suggesting image/text extensions. It is a short theoretical report without the target's scientific applications, but anticipates dual-space avoidance of explicit boundary reflection.

competitive_landscape.title: Mirror Diffusion Models for Constrained and Watermarked Generation
competitive_landscape.difference: Liu et al. map convex constrained sets to an unconstrained Euclidean dual space so transition kernels and scores remain tractable, derive efficient maps for simplices and l2 balls, and report improvements over prior constrained methods. It trades the target's direct barrier/reflection geometry and general manifold aspiration for analytic training and stronger convex-domain scalability.

competitive_landscape.title: Reflected Schrodinger Bridge for Constrained Generative Modeling
competitive_landscape.difference: Deng et al. add entropy-regularized optimal transport, reflected forward-backward SDEs, Neumann/Robin boundary conditions, likelihood training, and an approximate convergence account, with image-scale evaluation. The target supplies two simpler noising processes and earlier scientific examples but no transport optimality or comparable scale.

competitive_landscape.title: Constrained Synthesis with Projected Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Christopher et al. recast reverse diffusion as constrained optimization and certify convex, nonconvex, ODE, materials, motion, and planning constraints. It targets feasible synthesis from existing diffusion processes rather than learning a constraint-preserving forward process, covering broader constraint forms at the cost of a different distributional objective.

competitive_landscape.title: Score-based constrained generative modeling via Langevin diffusions with boundary conditions
competitive_landscape.difference: Nordenhog and Sharma introduce underdamped kinetic Langevin dynamics with specular velocity reflection, characterize its reverse boundary dynamics, and give optimally convergent discretizations while directly comparing local-time reflected models. This addresses sampler regularity and rate questions left open by the reviewed Brownian constructions.

competitive_landscape.title: Reflected Schrodinger Bridge Matching
competitive_landscape.difference: Haggbom et al. give a partially simulation-free reflected bridge framework with a new regression target and report negligible extra wall-clock cost on high-dimensional image couplings. It directly attacks the full-path simulation and higher-derivative burden of earlier reflected bridge methods; the reviewed paper remains simpler but substantially less scalable and less rigorously benchmarked.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the first principled extension of continuous diffusion models to inequality-constrained manifolds, offering complementary log-barrier and reflected-Brownian noising processes together with reverse dynamics, score matching, discretizations, likelihood evaluation, and scientific applications.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The target combines an interior Hessian-metric construction, a reflected construction, a boundary-aware implicit-score recipe, and demonstrations on polytopes, trace-constrained SPD factors, a robot manipulability trajectory, and a peptide polytope-torus product. At publication, ordinary Riemannian score models did not handle boundaries, and the exact barrier-plus-reflection scientific package was distinct. However, Reflected Diffusion Models was submitted one day earlier and independently supplied a broader and more scalable reflected score/ODE/likelihood treatment; the target's own later Metropolis work and mirror, projected, bridge, and kinetic methods quickly improved its sampler limitations.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The durable novelty is the paired geometric design space and its early scientific proof-of-concept: constraints can be encoded as a diverging metric or as reflection, and product constructions can combine a bounded factor with an ordinary manifold. The stronger novelty and rigor claims do not survive close audit. Reflected diffusion and its ODE were concurrent, the barrier and reflection proofs contain material contradictions, the implemented boundary condition is biased, high-dimensional synthetic fidelity loses badly to Euclidean diffusion, and the artifact does not identify an executable reproduction. This paper is best read as an influential construction/hypothesis paper whose mathematical statements need correction and whose original samplers have been practically superseded, not as a complete validated solution for general constrained manifolds.

reviewer_notes: The official arXiv record checked on 2026-08-24 remains v2, revised 2024-03-07, and identifies the work as published in TMLR in July 2023. The pinned PDF and indexed extraction cover all 36 pages with no missing-text page. Visual inspection covered every page at rendered resolution, including small pair plots, trajectory panels, score fields, pseudocode, Table 1, and all proof equations. Main-paper pages are 1-13, references 14-18, and supplement 19-36. The exact source archive contains TeX and assets but no executable experiment bundle. Static artifact audit used the paper-linked https://github.com/oxcsml/constrained-diffusion at public HEAD fbeee12df178ed2e08dd0596e791f0d32a3a8c6a, one commit dated 2023-08-15, and its required oxcsml/geomstats tmlr branch at b1b23a3be8c7209fa69376fa02779b306dc66b8c, dated 2023-07-24. No research code, dependency, dataset, or checkpoint was executed. Python 3 syntax compilation alone exposed an incomplete import in run_product.py and IPython magics in multiple .py scripts/tests. The release has included NPZ/CSV data and readable core SDE/loss/config modules, but no tags, license, pinned environment, CI, complete result assets, exact commands, or clean install; requirements/setup/config defects and a committed plaintext W&B credential further preclude treating it as a turnkey artifact. Appendix J's claimed batch-size-256, 100k-step, beta_max=6 recipe conflicts materially with checked task configs. The exact source's peptide appendix actively derives and trains on T^3 while figures, main text, code config, and full pair plot use four torus coordinates. All claims are separated into author reports, reviewer inferences, and contradiction audits. No shared generated atlas data was rebuilt, and no repository file other than this claimed reading was authored.
